title: Enhanced quantum metrology with robust multipass interferometry
authors: Sayak Mukherjee, José Afonso Oliveira, Sean William Moore, Jacob A. Dunningham
abstract: Quantum metrology typically uses entangled states to achieve measurement precisions beyond the standard quantum limit. The advantage increases with the size of the entangled state, however generating and preserving large entangled states remains a major experimental challenge. Multipass protocols offer an alternative approach by allowing a single probe to interact repeatedly with the parameter of interest, but their performance is highly susceptible to loss, which accumulates over successive passes and rapidly erodes the quantum advantage. Here we introduce a hybrid strategy that combines small, loss-resilient entangled states with multipass interferometry. We show that this approach retains the robustness of small entangled probes while exploiting repeated interactions to achieve substantial enhancements in measurement precision. Furthermore, we propose a concrete implementation using currently available technologies, demonstrating that the predicted performance gains should be experimentally accessible with existing capabilities.
summary: This paper proposes a hybrid quantum metrology technique that merges the benefits of multipass interferometry with the robustness of small entangled states. By analyzing the Quantum Fisher Information under realistic loss models, the authors demonstrate that a 'rotated NOON state' approach significantly enhances measurement precision compared to standard methods. This offers a practical pathway toward achieving quantum-enhanced sensing using current experimental technology.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving measurement precisions beyond the standard quantum limit in realistic quantum metrology setups, particularly when particle loss and decoherence are present.
main_result: A hybrid strategy combining small, loss-resilient entangled states with multipass interferometry significantly outperforms standard NOON-state or single-photon multipass schemes under realistic loss conditions.
method: The authors analyze the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and Classical Fisher Information ($F_C$) to determine the ultimate measurement precision limit ($\delta\phi$).
model_or_system: The model is a Mach-Zehnder interferometer incorporating a multipass element in one arm, where loss is modeled by imperfect mirror reflectivity ($\eta < 1$).
key_observables: Measurement precision ($\delta\phi$), Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q$), and Classical Fisher Information ($F_C$).
important_parameters: Number of particles ($N$), number of passes ($p$), and the loss parameter ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes asymptotic estimation theory applies and that loss occurs primarily in the sensing arm.
figures_summary: Figures compare the scaling of $F_Q/(Np)$ and $F_C/(Np)$ for various states (NOON, BAT, Rotated NOON) versus the number of passes ($p$), demonstrating the superiority of the rotated NOON state.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical limits (Heisenberg scaling) to analyzing the failure modes of large entangled states and single-photon schemes due to loss. It then introduces and analyzes the hybrid strategy using rotated NOON states and multipass interferometry.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum enhancement in optical systems, providing concrete, loss-robust protocols that are highly relevant to experimental quantum optics and sensing.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The multipass Mach-Zehnder interferometer consisting of two 50:50 beam splitters, two mirrors, photon number counting detectors D1 and D2 and an optical cavity. The upper path is passed multiple times through the sample in the cavity, accumulating a phase, ϕ, each time. Environmental losses are modelled by considering the cavity mirrors to be leaky with a reflection probability of η.

FIG. 2. The quantum Fisher information per particle-pass, FQ/(Np), is shown as a function of the number of passes, p, for NOON states with N = 1, 2, 5. In each case η = 0.95. All the different sized NOON states achieve the same maximum value.

FIG. 3. FQ/(Np) plotted as a function of p for different states. The general state (8) with optimised coefficients is shown as the blue line. This is compared with the other states discussed in the text. In each case N = 4 and η = 0.95.

FIG. 4. The results of Fig. 3 – redisplayed with a different p range and the optimised state removed – are compared with the rotated NOON state. The rotated NOON state outperforms all the other states. For the parameters used here, N = 4 and η = 0.95, the optimal number of passes is p = 17 and the optimal beam splitter reflectivity is 0.83.

FIG. 6. maxp FC/(Np) is plotted as a function of η, the per-pass transmission. There is a clear hierarchy where the rotated NOON dominates the BAT which in turn dominates the NOON for all η displayed.
